one_line: Camera-plus-POS exception alerts (self-checkout non-scans, back-door/receiving shrink, cash-wrap anomalies) that queue short clips for a human to review — no face recognition, no audio, no autonomous accusations.

problem.summary: Independent grocers, liquor stores, pharmacies, hardware stores and convenience stores lose roughly 1.5-2% of sales to shrink, and the two largest buckets are internal and external theft plus process error at checkout and receiving. Self-checkout, which even small stores now install to save labor, measurably raises loss (mean +22% in the year after installation across 8 grocery chains / 1,300 stores), and the loss shows up as unscanned items, wrong items and walk-aways that no one sees because the attendant is also running customer service. Today the work is done by hand: a manager scrubs a DVR after a complaint, a receiver trusts the vendor's count, and a cashier's voids and no-sales are never compared to video. The expensive part is not cameras — it is the human attention needed to watch and the risk of getting it wrong when a clerk acts on a hunch.

evidence.fact: US retail shrink averaged 1.6% of sales in FY2022, $112.1 billion, up from 1.4% / $93.9 billion in FY2021; internal and external theft together were about 65% of shrink.
41% of surveyed retailers said no employee is authorized to stop or apprehend a shoplifter (up from 38%), so detection value now comes from documentation and deterrence, not confrontation.
Self-checkout raised loss by a mean of 22% in the year after installation (range 3.19%-41.2%) across 8 grocery retailers and 1,300 test stores; average difference of +0.26 percentage points of sales.
Missed scans were the most frequent self-checkout loss behavior, at 1%-4.8% of transactions, in data supplied by 39 retailers with combined turnover over EUR 1 trillion.

Retailers' own estimates of how much non-scan behavior is malicious ranged from 6% to 80%, which the authors read as evidence that intent estimates are unreliable — i.e. most alerts are not proof of theft.

Middlesex County has 2,280 retail establishments (NAICS 44-45) with 37,013 employees and average annual pay of $45,485; grocery stores alone are 333 establishments / 7,002 employees and beer-wine-liquor stores 143 establishments / 945 employees at $30,985 average pay.

False-positive-driven accusations are a documented, government-charged harm: the FTC alleged Rite Aid's system generated thousands of false matches from 2012-2020, and employees followed, searched, ordered out or called police on wrongly flagged customers, disproportionately people of color.

New Jersey upgraded retail-theft crimes and created a retail-theft unit in the Department of Law and Public Safety (A4755/S3587 signed April 1, 2025), which raises the value of clean, timestamped incident evidence a small store can hand to police.

buyers.size_where_it_matters: 8-200 staff, one or more self-checkout lanes, $3M+ annual sales
buyers.why: Highest exposure to non-scan and produce PLU fraud; 186 supermarkets and 5,902 grocery employees in Middlesex County; already has a POS and cameras, so incremental cost is analytics only.

High value per item (spirits), low staff density, single-counter layout; 143 establishments / 945 employees in the county and the lowest average pay ($30,985), so there is no budget for dedicated watchers.
OTC and high-theft SKUs plus a controlled-substance compliance culture; 198 establishments / 2,145 employees in the county; already comfortable with camera systems and audit trails.

buyers.size_where_it_matters: 5-100 staff with a loading dock or back-door receiving
buyers.why: Bulky, high-ticket items and contractor traffic make receiving-count and back-door control the weak point; 94 building-material establishments / 2,741 employees in the county.
Small baskets, cash, high-turnover staff, single clerk on duty — cash-wrap voids/refunds and sweethearting are the main leaks; 96 establishments / 1,304 employees in the county.

buyers.business_type: Small general merchandise / dollar-format variety store
buyers.why: Broad low-value assortment, self-checkout, thin staffing; 129 establishments / 7,131 employees in the county — the segment where a chain's LP software is priced out of reach.

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Vision AI on existing checkout/self-checkout cameras plus POS data to detect non-scans, mis-scans and product switching, prompting the shopper or attendant in real time; extended to store-wide analytics.
existing_solutions.pricing: Unknown (not published; quote by store count and modules)

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Analyses self-checkout and staffed-lane video against POS transaction data to flag scan avoidance, bottom-of-basket loss and sweethearting.
Cloud VMS with AI people/vehicle analytics, POS overlay and alerting; the clearest public price anchor in the category.
existing_solutions.pricing: Public: $399 per camera (R120 mini dome) plus $149/camera/year Professional licence; AI features and cloud archiving not included in Professional

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Cloud video with POS transaction overlay, exception search and loss-prevention case workflows aimed at multi-site retail and restaurants.
existing_solutions.pricing: Unknown (FAQ says quotes vary with camera count, resolution and retention)

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Ingests POS, inventory, HR and alarm data to surface transaction exceptions (voids, refunds, no-sales, discounts) and route them to stores for follow-up.

existing_solutions.product: Local NVR with object detection, tracking, zones and a review queue
existing_solutions.what_it_does: Runs on your own hardware, defines zones and required-zone review items, records clips, integrates with Home Assistant/MQTT. Cannot add custom labels, so it is a strong base layer but not a product-level scan detector.
existing_solutions.pricing: Frigate free/open source; Frigate+ is an annual subscription (12 fine-tunes included, extra fine-tunes $5); exact subscription price not shown in the page text I read

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Detector-and-tracker toolkit for custom object/person models and zone analytics; the practical build block for a bespoke installer.
existing_solutions.pricing: Public: Pro $29/seat/month; Enterprise licence custom-priced. Community licence is AGPL-3.0, so a closed commercial deployment needs the Enterprise licence

gap_for_local_installer: The named vision-AI loss vendors sell to chains: Everseen, NCR and Agilence publish no price and are built around enterprise POS/SCO estates, while Rhombus-class cloud cameras start around $548 per camera in year one and do not do item-level scan detection. A 5-50 staff store in Middlesex County is too small for a chain contract and too complex for a $200 consumer kit. The open gap is a local integrator that (a) installs 4-12 cameras on a local box so no video leaves the store, (b) joins them to whatever POS the store already runs (Square, Clover, NCR, Lightspeed) using daily exports if there is no API, (c) tunes zone rules for that store's actual back door, receiving bay and cash wrap, and (d) delivers a short daily human-review queue with a written escalation policy that forbids acting on an unreviewed alert. That is a service business (install + calibration + monthly review support), not a product.

technical_approach.established_pattern: IP cameras -> local NVR running a person/object detector plus multi-object tracker -> zone and line-crossing rules per camera (each SCO lane, the bagging area, back door inside/outside, receiving dock, cash-wrap till) -> fusion with transaction events (POS export or SCO scan events) -> exception scoring and de-duplication -> short clip + still queued for human review -> reviewer confirms or rejects, and rejections feed back as training negatives. A small vision-language model is used only as a second stage on flagged clips (describe what is in the basket or hands, read a receipt or label), never as the primary alarm. This mirrors how the published systems work: YOLO-family detection plus tracking for people and objects, and POS-video comparison for lane-level events.

models_and_tools.name: Ultralytics YOLO (YOLO11/YOLO26 family) + ByteTrack/BoT-SORT
models_and_tools.role: Person and object detection and tracking; ByteTrack is the lightweight default for static overhead cameras, BoT-SORT adds camera-motion compensation and optional ReID.

models_and_tools.name: Frigate
models_and_tools.role: Local NVR, camera management, zones with required-zone review items, clip retention, MQTT/Home Assistant hooks. Base layer only: custom labels are not supported.

models_and_tools.name: Liquid AI LFM2-VL-450M / 1.6B
models_and_tools.role: Small vision-language check on flagged clips (e.g. 'is there an unscanned item in the bagging area?'), designed for low-latency edge deployment; GGUF builds run under llama.cpp.

models_and_tools.name: Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct
models_and_tools.role: Stronger VLM when the store has a Jetson-class GPU and reviewer volume justifies it; 4B GGUF quantisations exist for local inference.

models_and_tools.name: llama.cpp (mtmd)
models_and_tools.role: Runs the VLM locally on the store box or a small GPU server; no cloud dependency, which keeps footage and inferences on site.

models_and_tools.name: Cactus (optional)
models_and_tools.role: Quantization, kernels and inference engine for phones, wearables and small devices, with OpenAI-compatible text/speech/vision APIs — usable for a reviewer app that runs a small model on the manager's phone rather than shipping video to a cloud service.

hardware.item: Jetson Orin Nano Super Developer Kit (8GB, 67 TOPS) — local inference box
Google Coral USB Accelerator (Edge TPU) — cheaper detection-only option
Raspberry Pi AI Kit (M.2 HAT+ with Hailo-8L, 13 TOPS) or Hailo-8L M.2 module
hardware.approx_cost: $70 kit at launch; Hailo-8L M.2 module $89

hardware.item: PoE IP cameras (4K dome/bullet, 4-12 per store)
hardware.approx_cost: $100-200 each (inference from vendor store listings; Rhombus-branded equivalents list at $399 including licence)

hardware.item: PoE switch, cabling, mini-PC/NVR storage, UPS
hardware.approx_cost: $400-900 per store (inference — not price-verified in this research)

technical_approach.fine_tuning_needed: Split answer. Zone, loitering, back-door and receiving rules need no fine-tuning — a stock person detector plus zones is enough, and Frigate explicitly does not accept custom labels. Item-level scan-bagging detection does need a custom detector trained on that store's own camera angles and packaging, plus per-store threshold calibration against a labelled week of footage; there is no off-the-shelf model that knows 'this box of cereal moved from hand to bag without a scan'. Treat VLM prompting as configuration, not fine-tuning.
technical_approach.data_needed: Two to four weeks of footage from the exact camera positions at the exact focal lengths; a POS export covering the same period (transaction-level if available, Z-reports at minimum); 500-3,000 labelled clips per camera scene, skewed to hard negatives (re-scans, hand-offs, kids, bags already in the cart, employee assistance); a documented exclusion list (uniforms, break areas, restrooms) and a named reviewer. Plan on relabelling after the first two weeks of live false positives.

measured_outcomes.finding: Self-checkout raises loss by a mean of 22% in year one (range 3.19%-41.2%), and by +0.26 percentage points of sales; every extra 1% of transactions through SCO adds 0.030%-0.048% loss.
measured_outcomes.sample: 39 retailers (>EUR 1 trillion turnover); 8 grocery retailers / 1,300 test stores for the before-after estimate

measured_outcomes.finding: Interventions help but the evidence is thin: of 14 companies testing non-scan identification/nudge technology, 7 reported positive findings, one a 9% loss reduction, another $136m saved across 2,000 stores (0.13% sales increase) and a reported 4.5x return.

In live self-checkout data, 3%-10% of transactions generated a scan-error nudge or alert and customers self-corrected in 80%-97% of cases after a soft nudge — a direct warning that raw alert counts massively overstate theft.
Average US shrink was 1.6% of sales ($112.1bn) with internal+external theft about 65% of it; 53% of retailers raised technology budgets and 46% added third-party security personnel in response.

Facial-recognition alerts produced thousands of false matches over eight years and employees acted on them by following, searching, ejecting and calling police on innocent customers; the settlement banned facial recognition for five years and required notice, complaint handling and deletion.
measured_outcomes.sample: Hundreds of Rite Aid stores; FTC administrative action

measured_outcomes.finding: A YOLOv5 + Deep SORT pipeline with trajectory time-series classification reached a 92% median F1 for suspicious-behavior detection on shoplifting clips from the UCF-Crime dataset, with 8.45x faster inference than the comparison method.
measured_outcomes.sample: UCF-Crime shoplifting clips (benchmark video, not a live store)

measured_outcomes.finding: Sweethearting (cashier fake-scan) can be detected from checkout video by modelling hand/object motion around the scanner, but the authors note real systems suffer from large numbers of false alarms that waste manual verification labour.
measured_outcomes.sample: Grocery-store checkout video; method papers, no field deployment metrics in the abstract

measured_outcomes.finding: Vendor-commissioned analysis claims a 374% three-year ROI for checkout vision AI.
measured_outcomes.sample: Vendor-funded composite organisation model (Forrester TEI methodology)

legal_privacy.issue: Automated flags acted on by staff without safeguards can be an unfair practice under Section 5 of the FTC Act.
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: FTC v. Rite Aid (Dec 2023): five-year ban on facial recognition in stores, mandated notice to consumers, written complaint investigation, deletion of images/algorithms, third-party assessments, CEO certification. The order is about biometric surveillance, but the reasoning (untested accuracy, no false-positive tracking, no employee training, disparate impact) maps directly onto any alert system staff act on.

legal_privacy.issue: Biometric data collection carries separate FTC scrutiny even absent a state statute.
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: FTC Policy Statement on Biometric Information (May 2023): use of biometric information or biometric technologies can be an unfair practice where harms are not reasonably avoidable, and the agency asks whether less risky alternatives exist. A non-biometric design (no face templates, no voice prints, no gait ID) is the low-risk path.

legal_privacy.issue: Recording audio of customers or staff conversations in the store.
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: N.J.S.A. 2A:156A-4(d) allows interception by a party to the communication or with one party's prior consent; a store recording conversations it is not party to, without consent, is exposed to the civil liability in N.J.S.A. 2A:156A-24. Practical rule: disable camera microphones entirely and record no audio.

legal_privacy.issue: Employee and customer privacy tort exposure for camera placement and review.
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: New Jersey's intrusion-upon-seclusion tort, restated by the state Supreme Court in Friedman v. Martinez (2020), turns on intrusion into a private space plus conduct highly offensive to a reasonable person. Sales floors, checkouts, back rooms and loading docks are defensible; restrooms, changing areas and break rooms are not.

legal_privacy.issue: Is there a New Jersey statute requiring notice or signage for ordinary retail/workplace cameras?
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: I could not confirm one. Secondary sources state there is no New Jersey statute or regulation governing employer video recording in ordinary work areas, and that N.J.S.A. 34:6B-22 (electronic tracking notice, $1,000/$2,500 penalties) covers only tracking devices in vehicles an employee uses. Posting signage is therefore a policy choice and a liability reducer, not a verified legal mandate.

legal_privacy.issue: Criminal exposure for cameras in private areas.
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: N.J.S.A. 2C:14-9 criminalises recording where a reasonable person would expect not to be observed (restrooms, locker rooms, changing areas). I confirmed the existence of this offence only through secondary summaries, not by reading the statute myself.

NLRB General Counsel Memo GC 23-02 (Oct 2022) argues that intrusive electronic surveillance and algorithmic management can violate Section 7 rights, and that employers must show a legitimate business justification and minimal intrusion. Practical implication: no covert cameras aimed at organising activity, no using alerts to punish protected concerted action, and a written policy on what the system is and is not used for.

legal_privacy.issue: State biometric statute (BIPA-style) exposure in New Jersey.
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: New Jersey had not enacted a BIPA-equivalent biometric privacy statute; biometric bills (A1488/S3181, A1494/S3182) remained pending in the 2024 session. The New Jersey Data Privacy Act (P.L.2023 c.266, effective Jan 15, 2025) treats biometric data used to identify someone as sensitive data but applies only to businesses processing data of 100,000+ consumers, or 25,000+ while selling data — most 5-200 staff retailers fall outside it.

legal_privacy.issue: False accusation, defamation and false imprisonment risk when staff act on an alert.
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: No New Jersey statute or appellate case I found squarely governs AI-alert-driven accusations. The FTC complaint documents the harm pattern (public accusation, search, police call) that would ground tort claims; treat this as unconfirmed legal analysis (inference), not a cited precedent.

I found no New Jersey statute setting a retail video retention period. Recommendation is a contractual policy (e.g. 30 days rolling, exceptions exported and held with a case note), role-based access, and deletion on request from the store owner — this is a design choice (inference), not a legal requirement I could confirm.

public: Self-checkout lanes visible in Google Maps/Street View or store photos, especially 4+ lanes with one attendant.
Job postings for 'self-checkout attendant', 'overnight receiving', 'loss prevention associate' or 'asset protection' at a single-site independent.
Google/Yelp reviews that mention being asked for receipts, waiting for an attendant, or items not scanning (inference: indicates SCO friction and unattended lanes).
Recent local police blotter or news items naming the store or its block for shoplifting.
Store assortment: spirits on open shelves, OTC, power tools, infant formula, energy drinks — categories NRF names as organised-retail-crime targets.
Number of locations and rough square footage from the operator's own site (a 2+ store independent can amortise the build across sites).
Old analog/dome cameras visible outside and no camera over the loading door (inference from street-level photos).
Public liquor-licence and business-registration records (NJ ABC / county) to size the operator and confirm ownership structure.
walk_in: Count self-checkout lanes vs attendants at peak; note whether the attendant also covers customer service or the cigarette case.
Look for a camera directly over each SCO bagging area and over the cash-wrap till; absence is the sale.
Back door: is it propped, alarmed, on a camera, and is there a dock/count station with light?
Receiving practice: does anyone count cases against the invoice, or is it 'sign and stack'?
POS terminal type (Square, Clover, NCR, Lightspeed, legacy) and whether the manager can export transaction-level data.
Existing DVR/NVR brand and age, where the monitor sits, and who actually reviews footage (often: nobody).
High-theft SKU placement: razors, spirits, formula, OTC, tools — locked cases are a signal of prior loss pain.
Staffing and turnover: single clerk overnight, new faces weekly, posted schedules (inference: higher internal-theft and sweethearting risk).
Cash controls: who closes, how often drops happen, whether refunds/voids require a second person.

pilot.scope: One store, 4 weeks live after a 1-week install/calibration. Four to six cameras: two overhead on self-checkout/checkout lanes, one inside the back door, one outside the back door or on the receiving area, one on the cash-wrap/till. Local NVR and inference box on the store network; no audio; signage at the entrance stating cameras are in use for loss prevention and that alerts are reviewed by staff. Daily POS export ingested overnight (transaction-level if the POS allows, otherwise the Z-report plus void/refund/no-sale log). Output is a reviewer queue only: every alert is a short clip plus a still, marked 'unverified', and the written policy forbids staff approaching, searching or accusing anyone on the basis of an alert. Weekly 30-minute review with the owner on precision, alert volume and false-positive themes; alert types that fail precision are switched off, not tuned forever.
pilot.hardware: 4-6 PoE 4K cameras, PoE switch, Jetson Orin Nano Super (or Coral/Hailo if detection-only), 2-4 TB storage, UPS, small network cabinet. Reuse the store's existing cameras if they are IP and at least 1080p with a clean overhead view of the bagging area.
pilot.success_metric: Precision and workload, not 'theft stopped': (1) at least 60% of alerts confirmed as genuine exceptions on human review by week 4; (2) total alerts under ~15 per day so a manager can clear the queue in under 20 minutes; (3) zero alerts that led to a customer confrontation; (4) at least one documented, clip-backed exception per week in each of the three target categories (SCO non-scan, back-door/receiving, cash-wrap). Dollar shrink impact needs a full inventory cycle and is explicitly out of scope for a 4-week pilot.
pilot.cost_range: Roughly $5,000-$9,000 one-time plus $250-$500/month support for a single store. Assumptions: 4-6 cameras at $100-200 each ($400-1,200); compute and storage $600-1,200; switch/cabling/UPS $400-800; install and aiming 16-24 hours at $100-150/hr ($1,600-3,600); POS ingestion and rule/zone calibration 20-40 engineering hours ($2,000-4,000 at internal cost or a discounted pilot rate); monthly covers remote health checks, model/threshold updates and the weekly review call. Excludes the owner's own staff time and any POS vendor fees.
pilot.assumptions: Store already has a working network and at least some IP cameras; POS can export transaction or Z-report data at least daily; one named manager owns the review queue; no facial recognition, no audio, no cloud video by default; pilot pricing is discounted and hardware is resold at cost plus install margin; no claim of measured shrink reduction is made until a full inventory cycle is compared.

fit_score.rationale: Demand is well documented (1.6% shrink, 22% self-checkout loss lift) and the non-biometric design avoids the single biggest legal hazard in this category, which is worth real points. But local buyers are small and thin-margined: Middlesex County's 2,280 retail establishments average $45k pay per worker and liquor stores $31k, so a $5-9k pilot is a real decision, and many independents run one or two SCO lanes or none. Technical feasibility is only moderate because item-level scan detection needs POS event fusion and per-store custom training; zone/back-door rules are easy, product-level accuracy is not. Defensibility is weak: Frigate, YOLO and small VLMs are commodity, and Rhombus/Everseen can move downmarket. The durable position is local install plus POS integration plus a disciplined human-review workflow and escalation policy — a service moat, not a model moat.

risks: False positives leading to a customer accusation: the exact harm pattern the FTC charged Rite Aid over. Mitigation (review-only queue, no confrontation, written policy, signage) must be contractual, not aspirational.

Employee-relations blowback: staff read 'alert system' as suspicion. NLRB GC 23-02 signals scrutiny of intrusive monitoring; announcing purpose and limits before switch-on is safer than a surprise rollout.

POS integration is the real project risk. Independents often run Square/Clover with limited exports, or a legacy DOS-era POS; without transaction-level data, scan-bagging detection degrades to person-in-zone analytics.

Licensing trap: Ultralytics YOLO community licence is AGPL-3.0, so a closed-source commercial deployment needs the Enterprise licence; Frigate cannot accept custom labels, so a bespoke detector is mandatory for item-level work.
Commodity competition: Rhombus-class cloud cameras at $399 + $149/yr and NVR apps keep improving; a local integrator must sell judgement and workflow, not just detection.

Store economics: a $5-9k pilot plus $250-500/month has to be justified against a shrink number most independents do not measure precisely — expect long sales cycles and requests for proof from a neighbouring store.
Chain-of-custody and evidential quality: if clips are handed to police under New Jersey's upgraded retail-theft law, timestamp integrity, retention logs and access records need to be right.

Scope creep into HR: owners will ask the system to police employee breaks and productivity, which converts a loss-prevention tool into continuous employee monitoring and raises the legal and cultural risk sharply.
caveats: Shrink and self-checkout statistics come from large-chain surveys (NRF's 177 brands; ECR's 39 retailers) — I found no New Jersey-specific or small-independent shrink rate, so applying 1.6% and +22% to a Milltown store is an inference, not a measurement. All vendor outcome claims (Everseen's 374% ROI, the 9% loss reduction) are Low strength: vendor-produced or self-reported by retailers. Peer-reviewed detection accuracies (e.g. the 92% F1 benchmark result) are benchmark-dataset results, not live small-store performance. Pricing for Everseen, NCR, Solink and Agilence is not published and is listed as Unknown. Hardware prices are list prices at time of research and vary by reseller and stock. Nothing here is legal advice; the confirmed items are statutes, agency actions and one state Supreme Court opinion, and the 'confirmed: false' items are flagged where I relied on secondary summaries or on inference.
data_gaps: No New Jersey or Middlesex County shrink rate specific to independents; NRF and ECR data are chain-weighted.

Could not query Census County Business Patterns by NAICS for establishment-size distribution (the API requires a key); used BLS QCEW annual averages instead, which give establishment and employee counts but not size bands.

No peer-reviewed field study reporting a false-positive rate for self-checkout non-scan detection in small or independent stores; the closest public numbers are ECR's alert-rate ranges (3%-10% of transactions).

Could not read the New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs Data Privacy Act FAQ page directly (extraction failed); thresholds and effective date were taken from search-result content of that page and related summaries.
Could not confirm a Frigate+ subscription price from the pages I opened (page states subscription + $5 extra fine-tunes only).
University of Leicester's 2026 self-checkout summary returned HTTP 403 and was not used.
No New Jersey case law found on liability for acting on an AI-generated alert; that section is inference.
Everseen, NCR Voyix, Solink and Agilence pricing could not be verified; no vendor would be quoted without a sales contact, which is outside read-only research.
